a_T = rα has no square in r.

why.correct: Push 1 is perpendicular to the door, so its lever arm is the full 0.80 m: τ = r⊥F = (0.80 m)(30 N) = 24 N·m.

All four pushes are 30 N; the difference is the lever arm.

why.correct: τ = rF sin θ = (0.80 m)(30 N)(sin 30°) = 12 N·m. Equivalently, the lever arm is (0.80 m)(sin 30°) = 0.40 m.

options: Right: twice the lever arm × half the force = same torque.
The force is halved, which cancels the doubled lever arm.
The lever arm doubles, which cancels the halved force.

why.correct: The 20 N force pushes down left of the axle, turning the bar counterclockwise: τ = +(0.30 m)(20 N) = +6.0 N·m.
+6.0 N·m (20 N, counterclockwise) − 6.0 N·m (15 N, clockwise) + 2.0 N·m (10 N up on the right, counterclockwise) = +2.0 N·m.
Sum the torques with signs: +6.0 − 6.0 + 2.0 = +2.0 N·m. A nonzero net torque starts the bar turning in its direction, counterclockwise.
options: Right: the net torque is +2.0 N·m.
Pushing down turns the bar one way on the left of the axle and the other way on the right; count torques, not forces.

This sets the force equal to the torque. Divide the torque by the lever arm.

The arrow’s length shows the force’s size, not a distance.

why.correct: Torques about the left end: F_R(4.00 m) = (20.0 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(2.00 m) + (60.0 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(1.00 m) = 392 + 588 = 980 N·m, so F_R = 245 N.
Block: mg − F_T = ma. Pulley: F_T R = Iα = (½MR²)(a/R), so F_T = ½Ma. Adding: mg = (m + ½M)a, so a = (0.500 kg)(9.8 m/s²)/(0.500 kg + 0.750 kg) = 3.92 m/s².
F_T = ½Ma = (0.750 kg)(3.92 m/s²) = 2.94 N; check with the block: m(g − a) = (0.500 kg)(9.8 − 3.92) m/s² = 2.94 N.

why.correct: The string does not slip on the rim, so α = a/R = (3.92 m/s²)/(0.100 m) = 39.2 rad/s².

options: Right: a = mg/(m + I/R²) falls when I rises.
Less mass near the axle means more at the rim, so a larger I.
Same mass, larger I; the pulley is harder to spin up.
Inertia resists changes in motion; it does not balance a weight.

why.correct: Newton’s second law in rotational form, τ = Iα, gives α = (1/I)τ: a line through the origin with slope 1/I (or plot τ against α for slope I).
options: Right: α = τ/I is a line through the origin with slope 1/I.
Rearranged, α = (1/I)τ, so the slope is the reciprocal of I.
α grows with τ, so against 1/τ the points curve.
